classification.difficultyReason: Development: coordinate readings from two differently scaled graphs and explain why France's physically longer Winter bar does not establish a larger medal count. This links routine scale reading to the taught requirement to interpret each graph using its own scale.

content.prompt: Consider the graph of Olympic medals to the right.

spec.description: Summer graph above Winter graph, with equal physical plot widths and different numerical scales. Country colours match between graphs.
spec.mathematics: Horizontal bars: USA 46, Germany 17, France 10, interpreted as approved graph readings. Vertical grid every 2.5; labels 10, 20, 30, 40, 50; no printed zero.
spec.answerVisibility: Supplied graph visible; no added endpoint values or answers.

spec.description: Winter graph directly below Summer graph with the same physical plot width. France's Winter bar is physically longer than its Summer bar.
spec.mathematics: Horizontal bars: USA 9, Germany 14, France 5. Vertical grid every 1 to 20; printed labels 0, 5, 10, 15, with no 20 label.
spec.answerVisibility: Supplied graph visible; no answer annotations.

children.label: a
children.prompt: How many gold medals did USA win at the Winter Olympics?

answer.worked: The USA bar reaches 9 on the Winter Olympics 2018 scale, so USA won 9 gold medals.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Ali says, “France won more gold medals at the Winter Olympics than at the Summer Olympics.” Do you agree? Explain your answer.

answer.short: No. France won 10 in Summer and 5 in Winter. The axis scales are different.
answer.worked: France's bar reaches 10 on the Summer scale and 5 on the Winter scale. Since $10>5$, France won more gold medals at the Summer Olympics. The different scales mean the bar lengths cannot be compared directly.
